newsitem.title: USA: Soybeans drop further, gold hits 4-year low.
newsitem.headline: Soybeans drop further, gold hits 4-year low.

text.p: Soybean prices dropped sharply for a seventh straight day on Wednesday as traders continued to push prices lower as worries fade about tight supplies ahead of an expected bumper harvest this fall.
In other markets, gold prices hit new 4-year lows and dragged other precious metals downward. Oil prices closed firm as weekly industry data showed drawdowns in stockpiles.
At the Chicago Board of Trade, soybeans for July delivery closed 21 cents a bushel lower at $7.11. That price was down 76 cents or 9.7 percent for the week.

Prices were also down almost $2 from the 8-1/2 year highs at $9.03 set in early May when commercial firms scrambled to buy soybeans on strong demand from exporters and processors, who crush the beans into animal feed and industrial oils.

Since then, prices have fallen back on news that major processors like Minneapolis-based Cargill Inc will import cargoes of soybeans from South America to keep plants in the southern United States running before the September harvest.

This week's sharp drop was triggered by a government report on Monday estimating the largest U.S. soybean plantings in 15 years and by persistent talk that a major commercial firm may surprise the market and deliver cash soybeans against the July futures, a sure sign of adequate supplies.

"We're still dealing with the liquidation in the July," said Mark Weidner, oilseeds analyst with Cargill Investor Services. "With the commercials holding the short side of the equation, the threat of delivery is there."
Barge shipments of soybeans have been arriving in Chicago for the past week, feeding the talk about delivery.
Corn and wheat bucked the selling in soybeans, with July corn closing up 2-1/2 cents a bushel at $2.45-3/4 and July wheat up 1-1/2 cents a bushel at $3.24.
But analysts attributed much of those gains to a technical bounce in the markets after recent heavy selling. Weather in the Midwest continues to point to excellent crops this year.
"They're cutting in the St. Louis soft red winter area and the talk is of excellent, excellent yields," said Charlie Sernatinger, analyst for E.D. and F. Man Interntional.
"There are awesome, awesome yields in northern Kansas. They may have a record Kansas crop," he added.
Gold prices slid to new 4-year lows, dragging down values for other precious metals. Gold for August delivery at the COMEX in New York ended down $2.80 at $332.30 an ounce.

"The consensus is universally bearish in gold, and with producer hedging apparent against a backdrop of seasonally slow demand during the summer, any upward correction will likely meet overhead selling," said Smith Barney analyst David Rinehimer.

COMEX September silver ended down 3.3 cents at $4.645 an ounce, while October platinum at the New York Mercantile Exchange fell $5.20 an ounce at $406.70 and September palladium closed $1.80 lower at $174.50 an ounce.

Russia's metal export agency, Almaz, said on Wendesday it would resume shipments of platinum group metals (or "PGMs") around July 10 under a recently signed contract with Japanese traders. But analysts cautioned against too much optimism.
"Russia is not viewed as reliable supplier anymore," said Rineheimer. "Their own stockpiles are in decline and the PGM market is heading into a supply/demand deficit situation."
Russia supplies about 60 percent of the world's palladium and 20 percent of its platinum. But exports were suspended since December 1996, pushing prices sharply higher this year.

Oil prices closed higher in what traders called a technical bounce. Weekly industry data on oil stockpiles confirmed stocks being draw down and triggered profit-taking purchases of futures by speculators who had sold earlier.

Crude for August delivery at the New York Mercantile Exchnage closed up 22 cents at $20.34 a barrel. August gasoline rose 0.51 cent a gallon to close at 59.29 cents and August heating rose 0.08 cent a gallon to 54.92 cents.
"There are funds that were nervous about their short positions, and they covered," said Scott Ryll, trader and analyst with GSC Energy in Atlanta.
After the market's close on Tuesday, the American Petroleum Institute said U.S. crude oil stocks dropped 4.4 million barrels for the week ended June 27.
The decline was slightly steeper than the one-to-three million barrel fall expected by traders.
Gasoline stocks fell 1.2 million barrels, in line with market expectations, but output dropped only 154,000 barrels from the torrid 8.25 million barrels per day the week earlier.
